topic: Earthquakes: Epicenter, Focus, and Seismic Wave Properties (P-wave, S-wave, Body & Surface waves)
text:
Earthquake Terminology & Wave Classification:

  • Epicenter: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
  • Focus / Hypocenter: The point within the earth where an earthquake rupture starts (energy release point).

Two types of waves:

  • Body Waves: Generated due to release of energy at focus & move in all directions. Include:
    • P - waves (Primary waves)
    • S - waves (Secondary waves)
  • Surface Waves: Body waves interact with the surface rock & generate a new set of waves, mainly L - waves.

* Note on Velocity: The velocity of wave changes as they travel through materials with different densities.

* Note on Density: Denser material ↓ higher is the velocity.

P - Wave (Primary Wave)

  • Move faster
  • 1st to arrive at surface
  • Similar to sound waves
  • Travel through:
    • gaseous
    • liquid
    • solid
  • Velocity order: S > l > G (Solid > liquid > gas) with max velocity in solid.
  • Longitudinal wave (sound)
  • 1.7 times faster than S wave
  • Vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation.

S - Wave (Secondary Wave)

  • 2nd to reach
  • Transverse wave
  • More destructive than P wave
  • Travels only in solid
  • Perpendicular to the wave direction in the vertical plane
  • Doesn't pass through core

details.summary: Comprehensive notes on seismic waves generated during earthquakes. Covers the distinction between body waves (P-waves and S-waves) and surface waves (L-waves). Key physical properties of P-waves (longitudinal, fastest, travels through solid, liquid, and gas, vibrates parallel to propagation direction) and S-waves (transverse, slower, travels only through solids, cannot pass through the Earth's core, more destructive). Also highlights how wave velocity increases with the density of the medium.

mcq.question: Which of the following seismic waves is a transverse wave, travels only through solids, and cannot pass through the Earth's liquid core?
mcq.explanation: S-waves (secondary waves) are transverse waves and cannot propagate through liquids or gases, meaning they cannot pass through the liquid outer core of the Earth.

subject: Geography

text:
Earthquake

  • Sudden endogenic force
  • Energy released during earthquake is elastic energy
  • Natural earthquakes occur in lithosphere
  • 98% oceanic crust
  • 2% continental crust

details.summary: An earthquake is a sudden endogenic force; the energy released is elastic energy. Natural earthquakes occur in the lithosphere, with 98% in oceanic crust and 2% in continental crust.

subject: Geography

text:
Focus / Hypocenter:

  • Origin of earthquake
  • Point where energy is released

Epicenter:

  • Point on surface nearest to the focus
  • 1st one to experience the waves
  • Point directly above the focus
  • Maximum damage

details.summary: The focus (hypocenter) is the origin of the earthquake and the point where energy is released. The epicenter is the surface point nearest to / directly above the focus; it is the first to experience the waves and suffers maximum damage.

subject: Geography

text:
Surface Wave (L-Wave)

  • Last to report on seismograph.
  • More destructive.
  • Cause displacement of rocks.
  • Least speed.
  • Most damaging waves.
  • Large Amplitude.
  • P + S → L wave

Annotation: waves are not reported (in the shadow zone region).

details.summary: Properties of Surface (L) waves: slowest, most destructive, large amplitude, last to register on seismograph, formed by combination of P and S waves.

subject: Geography

text:
P-Wave

  • Seismographs located beyond 145° from epicentre record the arrival P-waves, ✗ S-wave (S-wave not recorded).

Shadow Zone

Diagram description (Earth cross-section): A circular cross-section of the Earth with a central core. Seismic rays emanate from a source point at the top. Two shaded wedge regions on either side of the core are labelled P-wave shadow zone and S-wave shadow zone. Angular markers are shown at 105° and 145° on both sides. Arrows at the base indicate "No direct P wave" reaching the shadow zone region.

details.summary: P-waves are recorded by seismographs beyond 145° from the epicentre, while S-waves are not. The P-wave shadow zone is depicted between 105° and 145°.

subject: Geography

text:
S-Wave

  • Entire zone beyond 105° does not receive S-waves.
  • Shadow zone larger.
  • S-Wave > P-wave (shadow zone of S-wave is larger than that of P-wave).

Diagram description (Earth cross-section): A circular cross-section of the Earth with a central core. Seismic rays radiate from a source at the top. A large shaded band across the lower portion is labelled S-wave shadow zone, bounded by 105° markers on both sides. A note reads "Not direct S-wave received here".

details.summary: S-waves do not reach the entire zone beyond 105° from the source; their shadow zone is larger than the P-wave shadow zone.

topic: Seismic Waves – Epicenter, Focus & Two Types of Waves
text:
Diagram (Earthquake Wave Propagation Model): A 3D rectangular block representing the Earth's crust is drawn with a set of concentric circles radiating from a central point inside the block. The central point is labelled Focus / Hypocenter (the point of origin of the earthquake within the Earth). A vertical line connects the focus to a point on the top surface of the block, which is labelled Epicenter (the point on the surface directly above the focus).

Two Types of Seismic Waves:

  • Body Waves – generated due to the release of energy at the focus; they move in all directions. Sub-types:
    • P-Waves
    • S-Waves
  • Surface Waves – generated when body waves interact with the surface rock and generate a new set of waves. Sub-type:
    • L-Wave

details.summary: Defines the focus (hypocenter) and epicenter via a 3D block diagram and classifies seismic waves into body waves (P and S) and surface waves (L-wave).

subject: Geography

text:
P-Wave (highlighted):

  • Move faster than other seismic waves.
  • 1st to arrive at the surface.
  • Similar to sound waves.
  • Travel through gaseous, liquid and solid media.
  • Velocity order (max velocity): S > L > G (Solid > Liquid > Gas).
  • It is a longitudinal wave (like sound).
  • 1.7 times faster than S-Wave.
  • Particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.

details.summary: P-waves are the fastest, first-arriving longitudinal seismic waves that travel through solids, liquids and gases, vibrating parallel to propagation and moving 1.7 times faster than S-waves.

subject: Geography

text:
S-Wave (highlighted):

  • 2nd to reach the surface.
  • It is a transverse wave.
  • More destructive than P-Wave.
  • Travels only in solid media.
  • Particles vibrate perpendicular to the wave direction in the vertical plane.
  • Doesn't pass through the core (because the outer core is liquid).

details.summary: S-waves are slower, second-arriving transverse seismic waves that travel only through solids, vibrate perpendicular to propagation, are more destructive than P-waves and cannot pass through the liquid core.

topic: Velocity of Seismic Waves & Density Relationship
text:
Note 1: The velocity of a wave changes as it travels through materials with different densities.

Note 2: Denser material → higher is the velocity of the wave.

details.summary: Seismic wave velocity varies with the density of the material it travels through; denser materials yield higher wave velocity.

mcq.question: Which wave is last to report on a seismograph and is the most destructive?
mcq.explanation: L-waves (Surface Waves) are the last to report on a seismograph, have the least speed, largest amplitude, and are the most destructive and damaging waves.
